title: Crime Stoppers funding requests received as information (2016 and 2017)
summary: Manitoba Crime Stoppers wrote asking for a grant in early 2016 and again in late 2017. Both times the mayor took the letter as information with no discussion.
status_detail: Received as information on Feb 2, 2016 and Dec 5, 2017; no grant decision is recorded in the transcripts.
figures: Amounts requested not stated in the transcripts.
public: Request letters from Manitoba Crime Stoppers (organization).
notes: Whether any grant was later paid through the city's grant policy is not shown in the transcripts.

title: Neighbours' speeding complaint on Hanover Street treated as a police matter
summary: At the Feb 2, 2016 hearing on a three-storey building on Hanover Street, neighbours said speeding on the street was already a problem. Councillor Fehr, supporting the project, said speeding was a police issue rather than something for council to address in the hearing.
status_detail: The development was approved; no speeding measure was attached and nothing further on Hanover Street speeding appears in the 2016–2017 transcripts.
reasons: rcmp-job: speeding is a police issue, not something council needs to address at a zoning hearing (John Fehr)
public: Neighbours (residents) told the hearing 'there's a speed problem' on the street; named only by first name in the transcript, so not identified here.
vote: development carried (one councillor opposed on height grounds, not on speeding)
notes: Traffic engineering is outside this topic; included only for the enforcement reasoning.

title: 2016 financial plan funds 16 RCMP officers and a community service officer
summary: The 2016 financial plan, presented at the Feb 16, 2016 public hearing, budgeted protective services (16 RCMP officers, a community service officer who enforces bylaws, and the fire department) at about $3.1 million, with the mill rate cut to 13.23. Council approved the plan with no policing debate; Councillor Zwaagstra moved it.
status_detail: Financial plan approved at the hearing; no member raised policing levels. The officer complement stayed at 16 into 2017.
figures: 16 RCMP officers; protective services (RCMP + community service officer + fire) approx. $3.1M in 2016; mill rate 13.23, down 1.07 from 2015 (transcript, 2016 financial plan hearing 0:01:21).
public: No questions from the public at the hearing.
notes: Seconder not audible in the transcript. No minutes exist for 2016.

title: Headway at-risk youth program asks the city for funding
summary: On Apr 5, 2016 the coordinator of Headway, a new multi-agency wraparound program for at-risk youth (RCMP, CFS, Hanover School Division, mental health, Addictions Foundation), asked the city to help close a $20,000 gap in its roughly $70,000 budget; the RCMP staff sergeant backed the request and asked for a yearly amount. The mayor promised a response under the city's grant policy. A written request (Jun 7, 2016) and an RCMP letter on Headway funding (Nov 21, 2017) were both taken as information.
status_detail: No grant decision appears in the 2016–2017 transcripts; letters were received as information in June 2016 and November 2017 (by consensus, Deputy Mayor Cari Penner chairing). The staff sergeant thanked council for its 'support of Headway' in May 2018 (outside this period; the form of support is unverified).
figures: Headway budget about $70,000, of which $18,000 in-kind from Hanover School Division and RCMP; $20,000 still sought (delegation, 2016-04-05 part 2, 0:09:19).
reasons: study-first: request to be answered under the city's grant policy and guidelines rather than on the spot (Chris Goertzen)
public: B.B., Headway coordinator, presented the program and cited Selkirk/Stonewall results (e.g. 50% drop in youth crime in Stonewall's first year — her claim, unverified). RCMP Staff Sergeant H.L. supported it and said council members on the RCMP Advisory Committee helped start it.
notes: The staff sergeant's 'Susan and Kerry' remark (0:16:20) names both Councillors Penner. The Nov 2017 letter's content and amount are not read out. Whether the city ever funded Headway is not shown in 2015–2017 transcripts.

title: Council reconfirms RCMP priorities: organized crime/drugs, visibility, property crime, traffic
summary: After the staff sergeant's April 2016 report, council passed a resolution confirming its RCMP performance-plan priorities first set in 2014: police visibility, organized crime (drugs), property crime and traffic. Councillor Funk moved and Councillor Zwaagstra seconded; both praised the RCMP and the GIS unit.
status_detail: Carried. The same four priorities were confirmed again on Sep 19, 2017.
notes: The seconder is heard as 'Councillor Switzer' (Zwaagstra). Exact wording of the resolution is not read out.

title: RCMP reports thefts halved, a meth problem and reduced traffic services (Apr 2016)
summary: Presenting occurrence statistics on Apr 5, 2016, the staff sergeant credited the city-funded two-officer General Investigation Section (GIS) unit for drug and theft results, said there was a meth issue driving minor thefts and mischief, and said RCMP traffic services in Steinbach had been much reduced by RCMP repositioning, so he had lobbied headquarters for more patrols. The mayor noted thefts and vehicle thefts had fallen by more than half from 2014 to 2015.
status_detail: Report received; council responded by reconfirming the same priorities (see 2016-policing-priorities). No council action on the reduced RCMP traffic services was taken.
figures: Thefts and vehicle thefts down by more than half 2014→2015 (mayor, 0:19:22); Steinbach–Blumenort traffic approx. 13,000 vehicles a day (staff sergeant, 0:18:08); 2-person GIS unit (0:20:08).
public: Staff Sgt. H.L. (RCMP) presented; said the meth issue had raised minor thefts and mischief and that targeted work was reducing them.
notes: When the GIS unit was created and what it costs the city are not stated in 2015–2017 transcripts (Zwaagstra says it had unanimous support). The occurrence statistics themselves were in the agenda package, which is not available.

title: Mental Health Act change frees RCMP officers from waiting at hospital
summary: On Jul 5, 2016 a Councillor Penner reported that a provincial amendment to the Mental Health Act, carried by Steinbach MLA and Health Minister Kelvin Goertzen, lets someone other than a police officer stay with a person waiting for a mental-health assessment. The idea came from the city's RCMP Advisory Group and the staff sergeant, who had found officers waiting hours at the hospital.
status_detail: Amendment passed by the Legislature (as reported to council); council recorded thanks. No measurement of officer time saved was reported in 2016–2017.
notes: Which Councillor Penner spoke is not determinable from the transcript (diarization also mislabels speakers in this file).

title: Funk leads a meeting with RCMP D Division on coverage for Steinbach
summary: The mayor said on Nov 1, 2016 that a meeting with RCMP 'D' Division (Manitoba headquarters) was coming at the end of November, spearheaded by Councillor Funk, as part of advocating for good RCMP coverage.
status_detail: No report on the outcome of the D Division meeting appears in the Nov 2016 – Dec 2017 transcripts. The officer complement stayed at 16 in the 2017 budget.
notes: What was asked of D Division (e.g. traffic services, officer numbers) is not stated.

title: Funk and Zwaagstra appointed to the RCMP Advisory Group (2016 and 2017)
summary: At the Nov 1, 2016 organization meeting the mayor reappointed Councillors Funk and Zwaagstra to the RCMP Advisory Group, crediting Funk with significant effort to 'advocate for good RCMP coverage'. Both were appointed again on Nov 7, 2017.
status_detail: Appointments made by the mayor (no resolution needed). The advisory group met the staff sergeant regularly (referenced Mar 7 and Sep 19, 2017).
notes: Earlier advisory-committee members appear to have included both Councillors Penner (staff sergeant, Apr 5, 2016; a Councillor Penner on Mar 7, 2017: 'when I was on the advisory committee').

title: Canadian Municipal Network on Crime Prevention event noted
summary: On Feb 7, 2017, with the mayor absent, Deputy Mayor John Fehr took a Canadian Municipal Network on Crime Prevention item as information and encouraged members to attend if they could, noting the mayor had sent a reminder.
status_detail: Received as information; whether any member attended is not recorded.
notes: The nature of the event (conference, webinar) is not stated.

title: 0.7-mill tax increase in 2017 goes entirely to higher RCMP costs after Steinbach passes 15,000
summary: The 2017 financial plan raised the mill rate by 0.7 to 13.93, and staff said all of the extra revenue would pay the higher policing costs triggered by the city reaching a population of 15,000. Council kept the same 16 officers; protective services rose to about $3.8 million. Councillors called the cost out of council's control; Siemens called it a 30% increase. The plan carried, with Zwaagstra and Funk voting against over the Performing Arts Centre, not policing.
status_detail: Financial plan approved in principle at the Feb 21, 2017 hearing; the 2017 tax levy bylaw followed (Mar 21, 2017 first and second reading).
figures: Mill rate 13.93, up 0.7, all of it for added policing costs (treasurer, 0:00:49); 16 RCMP officers; protective services approx. $3.8M in 2017 vs approx. $3.1M in 2016 (2017 and 2016 hearings); policing 'a 30% increase' (Siemens, 0:17:42). The rise in the municipal share (from 70% to 90% at 15,000 population, per the provincial policing arrangement) is not stated in the transcripts.
reasons: federal-sets-cost: the RCMP amount is out of council's control; same officers, higher cost (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: would have preferred to stay under 15,000 to contain policing costs; kept the rest of the budget frugal (John Fehr); cost: the big difference this year is policing; 0.7 mill needed to cover it (Jac Siemens)
public: No questions from the public at the hearing.
mover: Councillor Penner (Susan or Cari; not determined)
vote: carried; Zwaagstra and Funk stated they would vote against (over the Performing Arts Centre); count not audible
notes: The 2017 package was not available to confirm the RCMP contract amount. The 30% figure is Siemens's statement.

title: Manitoba Justice Community Safety Officer program referred to the RCMP Advisory Group
summary: A Manitoba Justice letter on Mar 7, 2017 offered its Community Safety Officer (CSO) program, piloted in Thompson. The city manager said no review had been done for Steinbach and that CSOs have limited powers. Councillor Funk noted the detachment already had two province-paid community constables who cost the city nothing and were taking over the D.A.R.E. school program; he offered to take the letter to the RCMP Advisory Group and report back. Council took it as information.
status_detail: Taken as information pending advisory-group feedback; no report back appears in the transcripts to Dec 2017.
figures: 2 provincially funded community constables in the detachment (Funk, 0:30:08); CSO cost unknown (city manager, 0:30:38).
reasons: already-doing-enough: two community constables already do similar work at no cost to the city (Earl Funk); provincial-responsibility: the province paying for the constables is the appropriate way; don't take away from what exists (Chris Goertzen); study-first: no review done for Steinbach; CSOs have limitations compared with RCMP officers (Troy Warkentin)
vote: received as information; referred informally to the RCMP Advisory Group
notes: 'Harold' is the staff sergeant (H.L.). A Councillor Penner (not determined which) also asked what the advisory committee thought (0:29:47).

title: Council keeps the same four RCMP priorities for 2017–2018
summary: On Sep 19, 2017 council confirmed the RCMP annual performance plan priorities unchanged: visibility of police, organized crime (drugs), property crime (break-ins and vandalism) and traffic. Funk moved and Zwaagstra seconded; Zwaagstra said property crime 'matters a whole lot' to victims.
status_detail: Carried. The same four priorities were confirmed again for 2018–2019 by R18-107 (May 15, 2018, moved Funk, seconded Zwaagstra), outside this period.
public: Staff Sgt. H.L. (RCMP) said these were the four priorities he would choose for a city of Steinbach's size.

title: RCMP: GIS drug unit left vacant for months by staff shortages; staff sergeant asks for nothing more (Sep 2017)
summary: On Sep 19, 2017 the staff sergeant reported steady crime numbers for the first half of 2017, more traffic charges and fewer impaired drivers. Asked by Councillor Siemens about lower drug enforcement, he said the city-funded GIS unit had been vacant for 3–4 months because of manpower shortages, with transfers coming. Asked by a Councillor Penner what more he needed, he said the city had provided the resources. He also mentioned a stop-sign 'coupons' education day run with the RCMP Advisory Committee.
status_detail: Report received; the GIS positions were expected to be filled in Sep–Oct 2017 (not confirmed in later 2017 transcripts). Council did not add resources and the staff sergeant did not request any.
figures: Jan–Jun traffic charges 237 (2016) → 323 (2017); impaireds 41 → 23; drug charges about 30 → 33; assaults 54 → 42; theft under about 110–120 both years; break-and-enters 38 → 37; mischief 108 → 112 (staff sergeant, 0:00:51).
reasons: rcmp-cant-fill-positions: GIS unit left vacant 3–4 months to keep general-duty shifts staffed while transfers were pending (Staff Sgt. H.L. (RCMP))
public: Staff Sgt. H.L. (RCMP) presented.
notes: Whether the GIS positions were filled is not confirmed in later 2017 transcripts.

title: 2018 budget raises taxes 0.16 mills, mainly attributed to the RCMP cost share rising from 70% to 90%
summary: Because Steinbach passed 15,000 people, its share of RCMP costs rose from 70% to 90% on April 1, 2017. The 2018 financial plan raised the municipal mill rate 0.16 mills (to 14.09) and the mover said it covered the last quarter of the higher policing bill. Three councillors voted against the budget, saying the real cause of the increase was a $500,000 golf course land deal, not the RCMP.
status_detail: Financial plan adopted 4-3 (R18-056). The 90% share was set by the federal-provincial policing framework once the population passed 15,000; council could only fund it.
figures: Mill rate 14.09, up 0.16 (transcript 0:00:58, minutes 4.3); ~$630,000 of the cost-share increase hit 2017 (Hrehirchuk 0:00:58); policing cost rose from ~$2.6M to ~$3.4M, ~$800,000 total, ~$200,000 in 2018 (Siemens 0:18:11); 0.16 mills = ~$150,000 (Hrehirchuk 0:14:47); protective services (16 RCMP officers, community service officer, fire) ~$4.1M (presentation 0:00:58).
reasons: federal-sets-cost: Crossing 15,000 people moved the city to paying 90% of RCMP costs; council had agreed new policing costs would come from new tax dollars. (Jac Siemens)
public: L.M. (Pat Porter Active Living Centre) asked about a grant in lieu of taxes; no resident spoke on policing at the hearing.
vote: 4-3 (against: Michael Zwaagstra, Susan Penner, Earl Funk)
notes: The minutes do not split the increase by item; the RCMP share of the 0.16 mills is the mover's account (about $200,000 of the ~$150,000-per-0.1-mill levy) and was disputed by three councillors.

title: Small yearly grants: Alternative Justice Committee ($200) and Headway fund ($8,000); fuel for Citizens on Patrol
summary: The yearly grant summaries list $200 a year for the Steinbach Alternative Justice Committee (2017, 2018, 2019 grants) and $8,000 to Hanover School Division's Headway fund (2018 grants), a program the RCMP commander thanked council for supporting. Citizens on Patrol told council the city reimburses its fuel.
status_detail: Grant summaries accepted unanimously each year (R18-065, R19-073, R20-064).
figures: Alternative Justice Committee $200/yr; Headway Fund $8,000 (2018 grants, R19-073).
mover: Jac Siemens (2018); Bill Hiebert (2019); Michael Zwaagstra (2020)
seconder: Cari Penner (2018); Susan Penner (2019); Jake Hiebert (2020)
notes: What Headway does was not described in the meetings; the RCMP commander mentioned a Headway worker classed as a rural employee (2019-04-16).

title: Council endorses a federal study of rural crime and RCMP resources
summary: At MP Ted Falk's request, council endorsed private member's Motion 167 asking the Commons public safety committee to study rural crime, RCMP staffing and shortages. Councillor Funk, then chair of the RCMP advisory board, moved it; members said the rural side of the Steinbach detachment affects the city.
status_detail: Resolution passed unanimously; the letter of support was to go to Parliament. No later report back to council was found.
figures: City pays for 16 officers; about 8 more are rural (Zwaagstra 1:19:33).

title: RCMP annual report (May 2018); council keeps the same four policing priorities
summary: The detachment commander reported 2017 numbers: most property crimes and impaired driving down, mischief flat, and youth stealing to buy cheap meth. Councillor Funk asked about meth. Council re-confirmed its four priorities: police visibility, organized crime (drugs), property crime (break-ins, vandalism) and traffic.
status_detail: Priorities for 2018-2019 confirmed unchanged (R18-107).
figures: 2016→2017: impaired driving 62→44; theft under 278→257; theft over 9→2; break and enter 91→81; mischief 233→234; vehicle theft 41→30; drug enforcement 64→57; 130 cell-phone tickets in April 2018 (delegate, 0:04:51).
reasons: already-doing-enough: Incidents were falling under these priorities, so keep them as they are. (Earl Funk)
public: H.L. (RCMP Staff Sergeant) linked vehicle thefts, mischief and shoplifting by youth to meth, "about $10 to be high for a day".
notes: Speaker labels G/D swap during the motion; only turns where the speaker was named just before are attributed.

title: Residents ask council to remove a walkway used by high-school students; council keeps it open and leans on RCMP and Citizens on Patrol
summary: P.F. and M.F. of Cottonwood Bend, later backed by a neighbourhood petition, asked the city to remove the sidewalk between McKenzie Avenue and Cottonwood Drive, citing vandalism, threats and loitering by students of the nearby high school. Council asked for a report. Administration said a storm sewer under the path meant it had to stay a public way, and listed options (school monitoring and cameras, RCMP patrols, restricted parking). Council agreed by consensus to keep it open, urge residents to call the RCMP, write to Hanover School Division and ask Citizens on Patrol to patrol.
status_detail: Removal refused; council chose reporting, patrols and talks with the school division instead. The issue returned in 2019 (see 2019-cottonwood-walkway-school-division-request).
figures: About a dozen incidents in 5 years (City Manager, 2018-07-17 1:48:48); storm sewer since 1991, sidewalk since 1992.
reasons: infrastructure: Storm sewer under the public reserve means the path must stay open; an unpaved path would be riskier. (Troy Warkentin); rcmp-job: Crimes should always be reported to the RCMP so they are on record. (Michael Zwaagstra); unintended-consequences: A closed or unpaved path would be more secluded and could become a better hangout. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: P.F. and M.F. (letter, June 2018) and a July 10, 2018 neighbourhood petition asked for the sidewalk to be removed; the 2004 version of the problem was resolved by RCMP work with the school.
vote: unanimous (report by end of July); July 17 direction by consensus
decision_source: minutes (R18-131); transcript for July 17 (no minutes on file)
notes: No minutes on file for July 17, 2018; the direction is taken from the transcript. Whether Hanover School Division was written to was not verified.

title: Councillors' own words on crime: "a safe city" with "crime issues", and support for the local RCMP
summary: In opening remarks, Councillor Zwaagstra described thieves entering his home and taking both family vehicles (Aug 2018), praising the RCMP response and calling Steinbach a safe city with crime issues to address. In June 2020, after the killing of George Floyd, Councillor Bill Hiebert spoke against racism and praised the local police force.
status_detail: Statements only; no decision was involved.
notes: Jake Hiebert, a former Winnipeg Police and RCMP officer, gave openings on police history (Jan 15, 2019; Jan 7, 2020); they contain no policy position and are not quoted.

title: Council passes on an AMM invitation to meet RCMP leaders
summary: The Association of Manitoba Municipalities invited councils to book meetings with the RCMP at its 2018 convention. Mayor Goertzen proposed taking it as information because the city already had a good relationship with its detachment.
status_detail: Received as information; no meeting requested.
reasons: already-doing-enough: Good relationship and communication with the local RCMP already. (Chris Goertzen)
notes: Meeting was three weeks before the 2018 election; the mayor asked whether to "send the next council".

title: New council makes Councillor Zwaagstra chair of the RCMP advisory group (re-appointed 2019 and 2020)
summary: At the Nov 6, 2018 inaugural meeting Mayor Funk appointed Councillor Zwaagstra to the RCMP Community Advisory Group as chair, replacing Funk, who had chaired it as a councillor. He was re-appointed in 2019 and 2020; two citizen members (T.A. and R.S.) were re-appointed in 2020. The group meets monthly with the staff sergeant, but its meetings are not public.
status_detail: Appointments ratified (R18-252, unanimous); re-appointed at the 2019 and 2020 organizational meetings.
notes: Minutes 2019-11-05 (organizational) item 9 and 2020-11-03 (organizational) items 10-11.

title: Manitoba Crime Stoppers grant requests filed without a grant
summary: Manitoba Crime Stoppers asked for grants in Dec 2018 and Nov 2019. Council received both as information; no Crime Stoppers grant appears in the 2018 or 2019 grant summaries.
status_detail: Received as information twice; not in the grant lists approved in 2019 (R19-073) or 2020 (R20-064).
notes: The amount requested is not in the minutes. No transcript exists for Nov 19, 2019.

title: Province's Urban Policing Grant received ($1.78 million in 2019)
summary: Manitoba Justice wrote about Urban Policing Grant support in Dec 2018 and confirmed $1,779,632.14 for 2019 in Nov 2019. Council received both as information without public discussion.
status_detail: Grant received; letters filed as information.
figures: Urban Policing Grant 2019 total $1,779,632.14 (minutes 2019-11-05 item 20).
notes: No transcript exists for Nov 5, 2019. The grant offsets a large part of the RCMP bill but was not mentioned in the budget debates found.

title: 2019 and 2020 budgets keep 16 city-paid RCMP officers while holding or cutting the mill rate
summary: The 2019 financial plan held the mill rate at 14.09 and the 2020 plan cut it to 13.70. Both kept 16 RCMP officers and one community services officer; protective services were budgeted at $4.2 million each year. Councillors cited the 16 officers as their answer to residents' safety concerns. In 2020 council also set aside $250,000 of the 2019 surplus for expected future policing costs.
status_detail: Both plans adopted unanimously; no new officer was added until council's Dec 2020 request.
reasons: cost: Held the line on taxes while the largest capital project in city history was under way; reserves set aside for future policing costs. (Michael Zwaagstra)
resolution_no: R20-094 (reserve transfers); 2019 plan per minutes 2019-03-19; 2020 plan per minutes 2020-04-07
notes: The reserve transfer text in the transcript reads "the city's committed" (a word is missing); the reserve's name was not confirmed.

title: Hanover School Division asks again to close the Cottonwood walkway; council refuses and studies 2-hour parking
summary: Hanover School Division asked the city to close the McKenzie–Cottonwood walkway. The RCMP advisory group, through Councillor Zwaagstra, recommended against closure and suggested 2-hour parking to keep students from parking nearby; council asked administration to study it. In September administration again recommended keeping the path open; the RCMP had heard few complaints in recent months, and council took the report as information.
status_detail: Closure refused (report received as information Sept 3, 2019). No decision on the 2-hour parking idea was found.
reasons: infrastructure: Storm sewer under the public reserve; path must stay open. (Troy Warkentin); unintended-consequences: Removing the concrete would leave a more secluded path. (Michael Zwaagstra); cpted: Crime prevention through design says closing areas off invites offences. (Earl Funk); low-crime: The staff sergeant reported few recent complaints. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Hanover School Division (letter) asked for closure.
notes: The mayor's 'SEPTA' is the transcript's rendering of CPTED (crime prevention through environmental design).

title: Fines for repeat false alarms raised; RCMP says the policy must come from council
summary: A councillor asked about 116 false alarms in three months and whether a fine would help. The commander said Winnipeg charges after three free alarms and that any such policy would have to come from council.
status_detail: No false-alarm bylaw or fee was found in 2019-2020.
figures: 116 false alarms in Q1 2019 (delegate, 0:15:35).
public: H.L. (RCMP Staff Sergeant): false alarms are "a huge waste of resources".
notes: The councillor who asked (Speaker F) is not named in the transcript and is not identified here.

title: RCMP report to the new council (April 2019): property crime down, same four priorities, commander asks for advocacy for more provincial officers
themes: priorities; rcmp-report; rcmp-complement; theft; drugs-addiction; advocacy
summary: The detachment commander reported break-ins down 8.3% and mischief down 15.7% year over year, a 60-charge break-in suspect caught, and detailed how provincially paid traffic, community constable and cadet positions cost the city nothing. He noted the municipal complement had grown by only two since 2001 and asked council to advocate for more provincial officers. Council re-confirmed its four priorities.
status_detail: Priorities for 2019-2020 confirmed unchanged (R19-096). No council advocacy for more provincial officers was found in the record.
figures: Break and enter 181→166 (-8.3%), mischief 383→323 (-15.7%) year over year; 16 of 25 detachment members municipal; 5-member traffic unit at no city cost; MPI paid ~$136,000 of overtime for 82 traffic initiatives in 2018; city accommodation share cut from 64% to 50% (delegate, 0:06:20 and 0:26:21).
reasons: already-doing-enough: The four priorities are as important as ever and fit together. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: H.L. (RCMP Staff Sergeant) said much of the drug and property crime comes from surrounding areas, and asked council to advocate for more provincial ("portable") officers.
notes: 'Portable guys' is the transcript's wording; from context the commander means provincially funded (rural) officers.

title: Citizens on Patrol report to council and seek volunteers
summary: Steinbach Citizens on Patrol (COPP), formed in 2008, described its evening patrols as the "eyes and ears" of the RCMP, its MPI seat-belt and phone checks, and its 9 volunteers (room for about 20). It noted the city reimburses its fuel. The mayor and councillors thanked the group and encouraged recruiting.
status_detail: Received as a delegation; continued city fuel reimbursement. No new funding was requested or given.
figures: 9 volunteers, could double to 20; about 2 shifts a month each (delegation 0:47:14, 0:52:21).
public: W.F., H.P. and E.N. (COPP volunteers) presented.

title: 2020 policing priorities renewed without an RCMP presentation (COVID-19)
summary: Because of the pandemic the staff sergeant sent the annual consultation form instead of presenting. Council re-adopted the same four priorities on the advisory chair's recommendation; no crime statistics were discussed in public that year.
status_detail: Priorities renewed (carried; no minutes on file for this meeting).
reasons: already-doing-enough: The RCMP accept council's priorities and are working toward them. (Earl Funk)
seconder: a Councillor Penner (which one not clear)
notes: No minutes file exists for May 19, 2020; decision taken from the transcript.

title: Council asks Ottawa for a 17th city RCMP officer, the first increase since 2015
summary: At council's own request, a motion went forward to apply to the federal Minister of Public Safety for one more officer under the Municipal Police Service Agreement, effective 2021. Councillor Zwaagstra noted about 1,000 people per officer, growth since the last increase, drugs and traffic, and that Steinbach has fewer officers per capita than comparable communities. The City Manager put the cost at $160,000–$180,000 a year. Council left where the officer is assigned to the staff sergeant.
status_detail: Application approved unanimously (R20-243). When the 17th position was actually filled is outside this period.
figures: 16 officers, ~1,000 residents per officer; last increase requested 2014, effective 2015 (Zwaagstra 0:10:57); $160,000–$180,000 per officer per year all-in (Warkentin 0:13:56).
notes: The minutes do not record the cost; the $160,000–$180,000 figure is the City Manager's estimate in the meeting.

title: 2021 budget: 16 RCMP officers and one bylaw officer, $4.2 million for police and fire, no tax increase
summary: The 2021 financial plan presentation listed protective services as 16 RCMP officers, 44 firefighters, 8 fire trucks and one community services officer for bylaws, budgeted together at $4.2 million. Council adopted the plan with the mill rate unchanged at 13.7; no councillor spoke about policing in the debate.
status_detail: Financial plan adopted unanimously (R21-064). Policing is not shown separately from fire in the presentation.
figures: 16 RCMP officers; protective services (police + fire) $4.2M; one community services officer; mill rate 13.7, unchanged (transcript 0:19:59; minutes R21-064).
public: No one spoke on policing at the hearing.
notes: The budget says 16 officers, but by Sept 2021 Zwaagstra said the city 'officially has 17'. Jake Hiebert said the 17th officer was considered 'last fall' (fall 2020, outside this period), and Zwaagstra said in June 2021 that an additional officer was being added. The 17th position was probably approved for 2021 but not yet counted in the presentation; not verified.

title: 2021 RCMP priorities confirmed unchanged: visibility, organized crime, property crime, traffic
summary: The detachment commander's annual performance plan report asked council to confirm the same four community priorities as before. Zwaagstra noted that break-ins had roughly halved, likely because people were home during COVID, and that an additional officer was being added. A Councillor Hiebert cautioned that police visibility can't be measured; Zwaagstra said it stays because residents want to see police.
status_detail: Priorities confirmed unanimously (R21-115). No numeric targets were set.
figures: Break-ins about half the previous year's number (Zwaagstra, transcript 0:51:10; RCMP report not in our files).
reasons: low-crime: Break-ins fell by about half, though he warned not to read too much into it because of COVID. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Zwaagstra said residents have long asked to see a visible police presence, which is why visibility is a priority.
notes: The resolution text says 'Community Priorities 2020-2021' while the acknowledgement of consultation is for 2021-2022 (minutes item 8.1). The commander was Staff Sgt. H.L. (initials per project rule for RCMP officers); he did not speak at the meeting.

title: Council asks the province for authority to install red light cameras on Main Street
summary: The same motion asked the province for authority to put red light cameras on Main Street. Zwaagstra, the mayor and (probably) Siemens all said they disliked red light cameras but wanted the option because the Main Street problem was serious.
status_detail: Carried as part of R21-195. No reply from the province or later council discussion of red light cameras was found in transcripts or minutes through Dec 2022.
reasons: provincial-responsibility: The city can only install cameras if the province grants permission. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Outcome with the province not found; check later periods or provincial correspondence.

title: After residents' street-racing letters, council asks for an 18th RCMP officer dedicated to traffic
themes: street-racing; rcmp-complement; rcmp-cost; residents; downtown; budget
summary: Three residents' letters on street racing (out of many emails and calls the mayor and councillors had received) were put on the agenda. Zwaagstra moved to apply for one more RCMP officer from January 1, 2022, dedicated exclusively to traffic enforcement, at about $200,000 a year, saying the 17 existing officers were too busy with calls and drugs to stay on Main Street. All members who spoke supported it; the officer started in May 2022, bringing the complement to 18.
status_detail: R21-195 carried unanimously. The 18th officer started full time in the week before May 17, 2022 (Zwaagstra), about four months later than requested. The mayor and Zwaagstra reported early results: impoundments for street racing, many tickets, less engine revving downtown. The metrics Zwaagstra proposed (tickets, complaints, collisions) were not reported to council in 2022.
figures: Cost about $200,000 a year (Zwaagstra and Siemens, transcript 1:00:47, 1:05:57); complement 17 → 18 (transcript 1:00:47; May 17, 2022 0:18:40); 0.4-mill increase in 2022 mainly for this officer (see 2022-budget-rcmp-officer).
reasons: cost: Not an insignificant cost, but the problem is significant and the city has to invest to address it. (Michael Zwaagstra); rcmp-cant-fill-positions: Existing officers are pulled away to emergencies and calls, so a dedicated position is needed for traffic. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Letters from residents B.U., S.M. and L.D. on street racing (and noise) were received as information; the mayor said there had been many more emails, calls and visits to his store. At a Dec 7, 2021 hearing residents E.W. and M.W. asked that the RCMP spend time at the Chrysler Gate/South Park three-way stop; Zwaagstra said the new traffic officer would not be limited to Main Street.
notes: The minutes record the three letters as 'received as information' (items 19-21) and name the writers; residents are given by initials here. Request date Jan 1, 2022; actual start about May 2022 (RCMP has up to a year to fill a new position, per Siemens and the mayor on Jul 5, 2022).

title: RCMP Community Advisory Group reappointed, chaired by Councillor Zwaagstra
summary: At the 2021 organizational meeting and the Nov 1, 2022 inaugural meeting the mayor reappointed Zwaagstra as chair of the RCMP Community Advisory Group, with two citizen members (T.A. and R.S.), the mayor and the staff sergeant. Council routinely refers residents' safety complaints to this group.
status_detail: Appointments ratified unanimously (R21-227; R22-244). The group's meetings are not public and no reports from it appear in the minutes.
notes: Citizen members given by initials. The Nov 1, 2022 inaugural appointments are from the minutes only.

title: AMM letter on the cost of the RCMP's first union contract received as information
summary: Correspondence from the Association of Manitoba Municipalities about the increase in RCMP contract costs from unionization was received as information without discussion.
status_detail: Received as information; no council motion, letter or comment in 2021-2022. (Council wrote to the federal minister about bargaining costs only in Jan 2025, per the existing report.)
notes: The RCMP's first collective agreement (Aug 2021) raised pay about 23.78% over six years, retroactive to 2017 (existing report, Global News); the letter itself is not in our files.

title: Crime Stoppers and Steinbach Alternative Justice funding requests received as information
summary: Manitoba Crime Stoppers' grant request and a Steinbach Alternative Justice grant request (Dec 2021), and a Crime Stoppers fundraising drive (Dec 2022), were taken as information with no discussion. The city's grants list shows $200 a year to the Steinbach Alternative Justice Committee in 2020 and 2021.
status_detail: Received as information each time; no funding motion found. Alternative Justice continued to receive a $200 grant (R22-066).
figures: Steinbach Alternative Justice Committee grant $200 in 2020 and in 2021 (minutes R22-066, Mar 15, 2022).
notes: The transcript says 'Manitoba Justice' for item 11C on Dec 7, 2021; the minutes show it was Steinbach Alternative Justice. Amounts requested are not in our files.

title: Resident reports thefts behind Whitby Crescent; mayor refers it to the RCMP
summary: At a variance hearing for a nearby apartment, resident N.P. described thefts from her home and a neighbour's, late-night activity, beer cans and speeding on Woodhaven, and asked about a fence. The mayor said theft and speeding were RCMP matters, asked Zwaagstra to raise them at the RCMP advisory meeting, told her to call police when it happens, and pointed to the coming traffic officer.
status_detail: Referred to the RCMP Advisory Group; no report back to council found. No fence was required (staff said buffering rules didn't apply between residential uses).
reasons: rcmp-job: Theft, speeding and littering have to be taken up with the RCMP; residents should call when it is happening. (Earl Funk)
public: N.P. (Whitby Crescent) reported thefts at her home 'more than once' and at her neighbour's; residents' reports, not verified.
notes: Already used in the existing 2022-2026 report (reason 5).

title: 2022 budget raises the mill rate 0.4 mills, mainly to pay for the 18th RCMP officer
summary: The 2022 financial plan raised the municipal mill rate from 13.7 to 14.1 (2.9%). The minutes of the hearing say the added RCMP officer and the events centre were the key factors; Zwaagstra and Siemens said the increase was mainly for the extra officer. No one from the public spoke at the hearing.
status_detail: Financial plan adopted Apr 5, 2022 (R22-076); tax levy By-law 2207 passed first reading May 3 (R22-107) and second and third readings May 17 (R22-124, R22-125), all unanimous.
figures: Mill rate 13.7 → 14.1, +0.4 mills, +2.9% (minutes Apr 5, 2022 item 6.7; transcript May 3 0:04:56, May 17 0:27:43). Officer cost about $200,000 a year (Sept 7, 2021).
public: No one appeared at the Apr 5, 2022 budget hearing (minutes 6.10).
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (R22-076, R22-107, R22-125); Jac Siemens (R22-124)
seconder: Jac Siemens (R22-076); Jake Hiebert (R22-107); Bill Hiebert (R22-124); Damian Penner (R22-125)
notes: The Apr 5, 2022 video has no audio, so the hearing discussion is from the minutes only.

title: RCMP letter on home cannabis grows referred to staff for a zoning review
summary: An RCMP constable wrote to council about cannabis grown in homes under Health Canada medical licences, asking whether the city could regulate it. On Zwaagstra's suggestion council agreed by consensus to have administration review the zoning bylaw and report back, and to raise it at the RCMP advisory meeting.
status_detail: Referred by consensus; no report back or bylaw change was found in council transcripts or minutes through 2022 (nor in later transcripts searched for 'cannabis').
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Medical licences come from Health Canada, outside city jurisdiction; the city can only look at zoning. (Michael Zwaagstra); study-first: Refer to administration for recommendations. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: The constable is named in the transcript; omitted here (RCMP officers by initials). Letter itself not in our files.

title: Cottonwood residents' complaint of squealing tires, racing and loitering leads to a daytime parking ban
summary: Residents of Cottonwood Bend and Cottonwood Drive, near the high school, asked for a weekday daytime parking ban because of cars squealing, racing and loitering. Council referred the letter to staff and the RCMP Advisory Group, then voted for the ban against administration's recommendation, saying the advisory group supported it. Siemens said the real issue was students gathering, not parking.
status_detail: R22-182 (Aug 2, 2022) restricted parking Monday-Friday 8 a.m.-5 p.m. on both streets, unanimous. On Nov 1, 2022 a neighbourhood representative thanked council and said it had 'greatly improved things'.
public: Letter from Cottonwood residents (signed F.H.) read at the May 17, 2022 meeting. On Nov 1, 2022 C.K., speaking for nearby residents at a rezoning hearing, said the parking change had greatly improved things.
notes: Mostly a parking/traffic item; included because the complaint was racing and loitering and council routed it through the RCMP Advisory Group. Staff said the idea had been discussed with the RCMP and Hanover School Division in 2018-2019. C.K. said 'last year' though the ban was passed in Aug 2022.

title: 2022-23 RCMP priorities confirmed unchanged
summary: Council again confirmed the same four priorities: visibility of police, organized crime, property crime (break-ins, vandalism) and traffic. Zwaagstra described D.A.R.E. drug education in grades 6 and 8, the General Investigative Section working on drug busts, and the new traffic officer, and said break-ins had dropped likely because of COVID. Siemens said the GIS had grown from one officer about six years earlier.
status_detail: R22-119 carried unanimously. Still no numeric targets; Jake Hiebert repeated that visibility isn't measured except through public feedback.
figures: Complement 18 including the traffic officer; GIS unit 2 or 3 officers (Siemens said 2, another member interjected '3'; transcript 0:20:40-0:21:05).
reasons: already-doing-enough: The four priorities 'are sufficient' and 'serve us well'. (Earl Funk)
notes: Commander was Staff Sgt. H.L. (initials); he submitted the report but did not speak.

title: Hanover School Division's request for a school RCMP officer: approved only if the division pays 100%
summary: Hanover School Division asked the city to request a community police officer for its schools, mainly the regional secondary school, with costs shared. Council agreed to be the conduit (school divisions can't contract with the RCMP) but only if the division paid 100% under a long-term agreement. Zwaagstra said the proposed formula would leave the city paying two-thirds; Siemens noted many students live outside Steinbach and regretted the request went to the press first; the mayor said once an officer is added 'you own them forever'.
status_detail: R22-170 carried unanimously with the 100%-cost and long-term-agreement conditions. No later council item on the request was found in 2022 (or, per the existing report, through Sept 2026); no school officer was added to the city's complement.
figures: HSD's formula: officer salary × 70% × 50%, which Zwaagstra said amounted to the city paying two-thirds (transcript 0:26:09). Siemens's proposed (withdrawn) terms: at least 3 years with 1 year's notice (0:28:36).
reasons: requester-pays: It is the division's initiative, so it should pay 100%; the city already added a traffic officer and won't add another at its own cost. (Michael Zwaagstra); requester-pays: Many SRSS students come from outside Steinbach; the division may get funds from other jurisdictions. (Jac Siemens); cost: Little benefit to the city; an added officer can't be given back, so a long-term agreement and notice period are needed. (Earl Funk)
public: Hanover School Division's letter (not in our files) was reported in the media before council discussed it (Siemens).
notes: Existing report quotes the 0:26:09 requester-pays passage. Whether HSD accepted the terms is unknown; in 2026 an RCMP special constable spends time in schools, but who pays is not in the record (existing report).

title: Citizens on Patrol says it is down to 8 volunteers and asks residents to join
summary: COPP Steinbach's chair E.N. thanked the city for its support, said the group had fallen to 8 volunteers from about 12-14, explained its non-engaging night patrols that report to the RCMP's non-emergency line, and said its funding 'used to be MPI, now it's kind of in limbo'. Council members praised the group and the mayor asked about ride-alongs; no motion followed.
status_detail: Delegation heard; no council action, funding motion or follow-up item in 2022.
figures: 8 volunteers, down from about 12-14 (transcript 0:37:21); members call the RCMP 'once or twice' a year each (0:41:20).
public: E.N. (COPP chair): city support is appreciated; funding formerly from MPI is 'in limbo'; patrols are non-engaging and act as eyes and ears.
notes: The kind of city support COPP receives is not stated in the record.

title: City joins the provincial Community Safety Officer Program to enforce truck weight limits
summary: On Feb 21, 2023 Adam Thiessen, Manager of Corporate Services, outlined the Community Safety Officer Program Agreement, which lets the city stop and weigh heavy vehicles to enforce road weight restrictions. Council voted to enter a self-funded program with the Province of Manitoba and the RCMP for that purpose.
status_detail: Agreement authorized (R23-036). The program is limited to vehicle weight enforcement; it did not create a general community safety officer force. No later report on its use was found in 2023-2024.
figures: Self-funded (minutes R23-036); no cost figure given in the minutes.
public: None recorded.
decision_source: minutes (2023-02-21 PDF; no transcript for this meeting)
notes: No transcript exists for Feb 21, 2023, so the debate (if any) is unknown; record is from the minutes only.

title: 2023 budget keeps 18 RCMP officers; police, fire and by-law budgeted at $4.6 million
summary: The 2023 financial plan kept the RCMP contract at 18 officers. Staff presented Protective Services (18 RCMP officers, 49 firefighters and one community services officer for by-laws) as a single $4.6 million line, so policing has no separate public figure. Councillor Zwaagstra, moving the plan, called the 18 officers a significant expense needed to keep the city safe.
status_detail: Financial plan adopted unanimously (R23-053). No change to the officer complement was proposed or debated.
figures: Protective Services $4.6M for 2023: 18 RCMP officers, 49 firefighters, 1 community services officer (transcript 0:12:14, Brian Hrehirchuk). Total operating expenses just over $34.5M (same turn).
public: None on policing.

title: New RCMP commander's 2023-24 priorities approved; council urges no warnings for street racers
summary: On May 2, 2023 the new detachment commander (G.L., three weeks in the job) presented the Annual Performance Plan with the same priorities as before: visibility of police, organized crime, property crime (break-ins and vandalism) and traffic, and described tickets and impoundments for street racing on Main Street. Councillor Zwaagstra, chair of the RCMP Advisory Group, confirmed the city was still funding the dedicated traffic officer and told the RCMP to give racers the maximum. Councillor Jake Hiebert asked why mischief to property had risen from 66 to 106; the commander said he would find out. Council approved the priorities.
status_detail: Priorities approved unanimously (R23-079). The promised explanation for the rise in mischief does not appear in later public meetings in 2023-2024.
figures: Mischief to property 66 -> 106 (Jake Hiebert, transcript 0:12:08); racing fines $672 each, 7-day licence suspension and tow (commander, 0:07:28); 5 provincial traffic members (4 constables, 1 corporal) work out of the detachment, paid by the province (0:11:20-0:11:59).
public: None; the commander urged residents to report racing, anonymously through Crime Stoppers if they wish, or by 911 if lives are at risk (minutes 6.4).
notes: A turn at 0:18:02 restating the priorities is labelled Zwaagstra but the speaker map flags a hand-off conflict, so it is not quoted. Bill Hiebert's question (0:13:58) is medium confidence.

title: AMM cities' resolution on the 'fair allocation of the costs of policing' received as information
summary: The Association of Manitoba Municipalities Cities Caucus (April 4, 2023) sent a resolution and request for support on the fair allocation of policing costs. On June 6, 2023 the mayor suggested taking it as information and council agreed without discussion.
status_detail: Received as information; no motion of support and no debate. Council did not raise policing-cost fairness again until its January 2025 letter to the federal Public Safety Minister (outside this period).
notes: The text of the AMM resolution was not reviewed (no 2023 package on file).

title: Council accepts the RCMP's 2024-2029 multi-year financial plan
summary: On July 4, 2023 the City Manager presented the RCMP's multi-year financial plan under the municipal police services agreement, which sets out the policing plan, systems and scheduled salary increases. Councillor Zwaagstra said most of it is set nationally and outside the city's control but approved it and said the city was pleased with RCMP service.
status_detail: Accepted unanimously (R23-140) and returned to the RCMP for filing. No figures from the plan were read out in public.
figures: No dollar figures stated at the meeting; the plan itself was in the agenda package (not on file).
reasons: federal-sets-cost: The plan is set at the national level; most of it is not under the city's direct control. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Provincial Urban Policing Grant rises; letters received in 2023 and 2024
summary: On Aug 15, 2023 the mayor reported a Manitoba Justice letter on the Urban Policing Grant, saying it raised the province's funding toward the city's RCMP costs by 28%. On Dec 3, 2024 a second letter set the 2024/25 grant at $2,562,436. Both were received as information; council did not discuss using the money for more officers.
status_detail: Grant received both years. No council decision tied the extra money to staffing or new programs.
figures: +28% provincial funding component for RCMP (mayor, transcript 2023-08-15 0:28:54); $2,562,436 Urban Police Grant for 2024/25 (Manitoba Justice letter of Nov 19, 2024, 2024-12-03 package PDF p. 104, described as 'the first budgeted increase in UPG funding since 2017'). 2024 police budget $3,806,868, $2,982,220.69 spent to Oct 31 (2024-12-03 package PDF p. 129).
notes: The 2024 letter calls 2024/25 the first budgeted UPG increase since 2017, which sits awkwardly with the mayor's 2023 '28%' remark; the 2023 increase may have been one-time or differently budgeted. The 2023 letter itself was not reviewed (no 2023 package on file). The Dec 3, 2024 item was not read aloud in the transcript.

title: Councillor Jake Hiebert's opening remarks on homelessness, parole and addiction
summary: Councillor Jake Hiebert, who said he spent 39 years in policing (including RCMP service) and six years on the Parole Board of Canada, used meeting openings on Oct 3, 2023 and May 21, 2024 (and Sept 17, 2024, see 2024-encampment-safety) to talk about crime and justice. He described homelessness he had seen as an officer and in Steinbach, explained parole, and argued for long-term mental-health and addiction treatment and for governments to act.
status_detail: Opening remarks only; no motion or council action followed.
figures: About 1,450 prisoners interviewed as a parole board member (2024-05-21, 0:03:32).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Long-term mental health, shelter and employment programs need trained professionals and governments willing to act. (Jake Hiebert)
notes: The existing report calls him a former RCMP officer; on Sept 17, 2024 he described 39 years in policing including Winnipeg beat work in the 1970s and the Vancouver drug section, and refers to an RCMP parka in 2023.

title: Crime Stoppers and Operation Red Nose funding requests received as information, 2023-2024
summary: Manitoba Crime Stoppers asked the city for a donation of 25 cents per resident in November 2023 and again in November 2024, and Operation Red Nose (a Crime Stoppers-linked safe-ride campaign) asked for sponsorship in November 2023 and October 2024. Each time the mayor proposed taking the letter as information and council agreed, with no discussion.
status_detail: All four letters received as information; no funding motion found in the minutes for 2023-2024.
figures: Request: $0.25 per capita (minutes 2023-11-21 item 14; Crime Stoppers letter of Oct 8, 2024 in the 2024-11-05 package PDF p. 110). At the 2021 census population of 17,806 that would be roughly $4,450 a year (our estimate).
public: Crime Stoppers' 2024 letter said police services are 'overworked' and that anonymous tips help solve crime (package).
notes: No transcript for Nov 5, 2024 (the 2024 Crime Stoppers letter); minutes and package only. Whether the city gives Crime Stoppers money through another route (e.g. the annual grants list) was not checked.

title: City joins the provincial Community Safety and Well-Being planning process
summary: After a Jan 9, 2024 committee presentation by the province, the Canadian Centre for Safer Communities and Headway, council agreed on Feb 6, 2024 to take part in a provincially funded Community Safety and Well-Being plan, aimed at improving well-being and reducing crime by coordinating governments and local agencies. Staff limited the city's role to a 'conduit' with up to 2 hours of staff time a week; the province pays the consultant and $60,000 toward a priority in the finished plan.
status_detail: Participation approved unanimously (R24-025). The plan itself was finished only in 2026 (see the 2022-2026 report); no plan or targets were presented in 2024.
figures: $60,000 provincial funding per community for plan priorities; staff time not to exceed 2 hours a week on average (Adam Thiessen, transcript 0:08:52); $1.3M provincial program across 12 communities announced spring 2022 (Zwaagstra, 0:12:01).
reasons: cost: Supported because no city tax dollars were involved, only limited staff time. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Headway (a youth and adult crime-prevention program based at the RCMP detachment) was one of the presenters at the January committee meeting.

title: Barbed-wire security fences: one denied, two approved to deter theft
summary: Barbed wire needs a variance outside heavy-industrial zones. On Jan 16, 2024 council denied one on a lot whose development had just been refused, after neighbours objected and Councillor Damian Penner said there was no security need. On Aug 20 it approved one for Manitoba Hydro's yard, a frequent target for copper theft, and on Sept 17 one for The Rental House's equipment yard, whose manager O.K. said the wire prevents theft and is required by its insurer.
status_detail: V-2023-25 denied (R24-010); V-2024-09 approved (R24-165); V-2024-13 approved (R24-181). All unanimous.
reasons: low-crime: Denied the Jan 2024 variance because the land had no projected use and so no security need, and neighbours objected. (Damian Penner)
public: Jan 16: several neighbours (initials only) objected for the record. Aug 20: R.K. for Manitoba Hydro said the fence was needed for 'site safety and security'. Sept 17: O.K. (The Rental House) said barbed wire prevents theft and lowers insurance.
seconder: Susan Penner (R24-010); Jake Hiebert (R24-165); Bill Hiebert (R24-181)
notes: Mainly a zoning matter; included because theft prevention was the stated reason. Bill Hiebert said 'Second.' on Aug 20 but the minutes record Jake Hiebert as seconder.

title: Residents raise theft, vandalism and speeding at development hearings
summary: At the Mar 19, 2024 hearings, two residents mentioned crime or enforcement while objecting to infill projects: R.B., a Second Street neighbour of a proposed 3-storey building at 331 First Street, described rising thefts and vandalism and items stolen from his deck; D.T., a Hospital Street resident, said speeding would justify a police officer on nearby streets around the clock. No council member responded to these points.
status_detail: No reply or referral on the crime points; the 331 First Street conditional use and variance were approved unanimously (R24-062, R24-063).
public: R.B. and D.T. (residents). Their accounts are their own and unverified.
vote: unanimous (on the development, not on crime)

title: 2024 budget keeps 18 RCMP officers; Protective Services rises to $5.1 million
summary: The 2024 financial plan again funded 18 RCMP officers and one community services officer for by-law enforcement, within a combined Protective Services line of $5.1 million (up from $4.6 million in 2023). No council member spoke about policing in the budget debate.
status_detail: Financial plan adopted unanimously (R24-073). The city's Oct 31, 2024 statement shows a police budget of $3,806,868.
figures: Protective Services $5.1M: 18 RCMP officers, 46 firefighters and 8 trucks, 1 community services officer (transcript 0:08:30, Brian Hrehirchuk). Police line $3,806,868 budgeted, $2,982,220.69 spent to Oct 31, 2024 (2024-12-03 package PDF p. 129). Total expenses just under $38.5M.

title: RCMP reports a big rise in addiction-driven break-ins; Headway presents; 2024-25 priorities approved
themes: rcmp-report; priorities; theft; drugs-addiction; vacancies; street-racing; youth
summary: On Apr 2, 2024 the detachment commander (G.L.) reported that break-ins and mischief had risen significantly, mostly by the same methamphetamine-addicted offenders, and blamed 'revolving door' release practices. He was one 'hard vacancy' short of 18, with leave positions not backfilled. He brought Headway's youth coordinator (H.H.), who reported about a 90% drop in justice involvement among clients. Council praised the drop in Main Street racing and approved the same four priorities plus a 'respectful workplace' objective.
status_detail: Priorities approved unanimously (R24-075). Council took no new step on property crime or addiction at this meeting beyond thanking Headway; the commander's offer to provide Headway statistics has no public follow-up in 2024.
figures: Break-ins up about 15% (commander's example, 0:40:33); one hard vacancy of 18 positions (0:46:03); GIS (drug) unit of one corporal and one constable (0:46:57); Headway: about or above 90% reduction in youth justice involvement (H.H., 0:55:27; minutes say 98%); first-year Headway cohort 17 of 19 stopped police contact (mayor, 1:00:23).
reasons: root-causes-elsewhere: Agreed with the commander on the 'revolving door' but said that is the legislation police must work under. (Jake Hiebert)
public: Delegations only: RCMP commander G.L. and Headway youth coordinator H.H. Headway's figures are its own and unverified.
notes: Letter D on Apr 2, 2024 is shared by the commander and Councillor Damian Penner; only turns clearly in the commander's presentation are quoted. Minutes give Headway's figure as 98%; the transcript says 'around or above a 90%'.

title: RCMP suggests a second dedicated traffic officer; council does not act
summary: At the Apr 2, 2024 presentation the commander said the dedicated traffic member was making an impact and that a second one 'would be even more effective', given new subdivisions, the events centre and 144 km of roads. Councillor Jake Hiebert, who said he had advocated a traffic officer for 20 years, said he hoped Manitoba Public Insurance (MPI) would pay for a second one. No motion followed.
status_detail: No council motion or budget change in 2024; the complement stayed at 18 (see 2024-financial-plan-policing).
figures: Speeding tickets rose sharply 2022 -> 2023 (mayor, 0:41:27); 144 km of city roads (0:43:27).
reasons: outside-funding: Hoped MPI would sponsor a second traffic officer rather than the city. (Jake Hiebert)
notes: Overlaps the traffic-congestion report. MPI-funded enforcement by Ste. Anne Police came in 2025 (outside this period).

title: Unbudgeted $550,000 drawn from reserves for policing in 2023
summary: When council ratified the 2023 reserve transfers on June 18, 2024, the list included $550,000 moved from the Committed Expenditure Reserve to the operating fund for 'Policing'. It was not in the 2023 estimate and was not explained at the meeting.
status_detail: Reserve transfers ratified unanimously (R24-126) without discussion of the policing item.
figures: $550,000 'Policing' in the actual column; the estimated column for that reserve totals $225,000 and the actual $784,054.70 (minutes 2024-06-18, reserve transfer schedule).
notes: Purpose unverified. It may relate to RCMP retroactive pay or a year-end reconciliation, but nothing in the 2023-2024 record says so. The City Manager described the transfers only in general terms (transcript 2024-06-18 1:35:59).

title: Main Street encampment raised as a safety issue; staff asked to research other cities
summary: On Sept 17, 2024 Councillor Jake Hiebert opened the meeting describing people living at the burned-out 447 Main Street property and others, methamphetamine use and thefts among them, and the need for long-term drug treatment. In question period Councillor Zwaagstra said residents and businesses saw the encampment as unsafe and asked whether by-laws could help. The City Manager said encampments are handled case by case with property owners, the RCMP and agencies; the owner had served trespass notices and the site was empty by Sept 16. Council agreed by consensus to have staff study what other municipalities do and report back.
status_detail: Referred to administration (minutes 18.2); no report back appears in the 2024 meetings. The city had no written encampment policy.
figures: About 12 people at two sites; 4 left at one by the weekend before (Jake Hiebert, 0:00:08).
reasons: root-causes-elsewhere: Homelessness is a community issue needing social agencies' expertise; the city only facilitates. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); already-doing-enough: Council's protective role is already met by the RCMP and a by-law inspector; asked how many tax dollars should go to social issues. (Jac Siemens); rcmp-job: A community safety officer works with property owners and the RCMP case by case. (Earl Funk)
public: Councillors relayed residents' and businesses' safety concerns; no resident spoke.
notes: Homelessness has its own report; included here only for the safety, policing and by-law angle.

title: Council takes no action on an addiction-outreach funding partnership; Teen Challenge request received
summary: Steinbach Community Outreach asked the city to apply to the federal Emergency Treatment Fund (only municipalities could apply) for a mobile outreach unit offering addiction referrals, counselling, naloxone and harm-reduction supplies. On Nov 5, 2024 council resolved to take no action. On Nov 19, 2024 an urgent financial request from Adult & Teen Challenge of Central Canada (a long-term addiction treatment provider) was received as information.
status_detail: ETF partnership declined (R24-215, 'take no action'); Teen Challenge request received as information with no funding motion.
figures: Proposed project Dec 1, 2024 to Mar 31, 2026 (2024-11-05 package PDF p. 75-78); budget described by the applicant as rough estimates.
public: Steinbach Community Outreach (organization) argued the program would make the public safer, e.g. by reducing discarded needles (package).
seconder: recorded as 'B. Siemens' in the minutes (no such member; likely Jac Siemens or Bill Hiebert)
notes: No transcript for Nov 5, 2024, so council's reasons for declining the ETF partnership are not on record. The City Manager's memo (2024-11-05 package PDF p. 73) warned that the city would become responsible for meeting the program's objectives and criteria if it applied. In his Sept 17, 2024 opening, Councillor Jake Hiebert had argued that safe-supply and food approaches do not solve addiction.

title: RCMP body-worn cameras roll out, billed to contract cities
summary: A Public Safety Canada notice said RCMP body-worn cameras would start deploying in the third week of November 2024, with contract jurisdictions such as Steinbach paying only once cameras are operational in their area (estimates on quarterly bills, credited at year-end). Council received it as information on Nov 19, 2024.
status_detail: Received as information; no cost figure was given to council.
figures: No local cost stated (2024-11-19 package PDF p. 82).
reasons: federal-sets-cost: Camera costs are added to contract billings by the RCMP, not decided by council. (Public Safety Canada (notice))

title: Administrative Penalty By-law updated so by-law officers can fine under new traffic and animal by-laws
summary: On Dec 17, 2024 council gave first reading to By-Law 2259, the Administrative Penalty by-law, which under the provincial Municipal By-law Enforcement Act lets the city issue penalty notices; it updates fines for the new traffic and animal control by-laws.
status_detail: First reading Dec 17, 2024 (R24-249); second and third readings followed on Jan 21, 2025 (R25-019, R25-020).
notes: Routine; included because it is the main by-law enforcement change of the period.

title: Letter to Ottawa asking for a say in RCMP pay bargaining
summary: Using an AMM template, council voted to write to the federal Public Safety Minister about the third round of RCMP collective bargaining, asking for slower cost growth and real consultation with the municipalities that pay the bill. Steinbach pays 90% of the cost of its 18 municipal officers.
status_detail: The letter went out January 10, 2025. The Minister of Public Safety replied on March 13, 2025 that policing is a shared responsibility, that provinces administer justice, and that municipalities are consulted through the RCMP Contract Management Committee; no commitment on costs. Council received the reply as information on April 1, 2025.
figures: City pays 90% of the cost of 18 officers; last contract gave a 23.7% retroactive raise (Zwaagstra, transcript 0:20:23); 21 Manitoba municipalities have RCMP contracts (transcript).
reasons: federal-sets-cost: Ottawa negotiates RCMP pay but municipalities pay the bill and have no say (Michael Zwaagstra); federal-sets-cost: easy for the federal government to spend other people's money (Susan Penner)
notes: Federal reply (Minister David McGuinty, Mar 13, 2025) is in the Apr 1, 2025 package p. 64; minutes item 38 'received as information'.

title: Speeding on Harmony Lane referred to the RCMP Advisory Committee
summary: After a speeding driver killed two dogs being walked on Harmony Lane, residents asked for a stop sign and speed control. Council ordered a stop-sign review and the mayor asked Councillor Zwaagstra to raise enforcement at the RCMP Advisory Committee. The engineer's review found no signage change warranted and called speeding an RCMP enforcement matter; the staff sergeant agreed to monitor the street.
status_detail: Feb 18, 2025: consensus to accept the report (no signage change). The mayor and Zwaagstra reported the RCMP agreed to put 'some RCMP detail' on the road. No enforcement results were reported back to council.
reasons: rcmp-job: speeding is an enforcement issue for the RCMP, not a signage issue (Troy Warkentin, City Manager); study-first: decisions should rest on the evidence in the traffic report (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: B.E. and K.E. (Harmony Lane) wrote that they had called the RCMP 'on several occasions and nothing helps because nobody shows up' (letter in the Jan 21, 2025 package; their claim, unverified).
notes: Mainly a traffic item; included for the RCMP enforcement referral. Residents' letter not quoted from the transcript.

title: 2025 budget: policing up about $400,000 with no new officers
summary: The 2025 financial plan kept the mill rate at 14.4 but raised policing costs by about $400,000 while keeping the complement at 18 officers. Councillor Susan Penner asked why; staff said the figure comes from the RCMP's own budget. Councillor Zwaagstra said RCMP costs are set in federal bargaining, and Councillor Damian Penner said police and fire were not on the table for cuts.
status_detail: Approved in principle March 4, 2025 (R25-048) and adopted April 15, 2025 (R25-082), both unanimous. Complement stayed at 18.
figures: Policing up about $400,000 (Hrehirchuk, transcript 0:15:17); Police & Fire Services $5.6 million, 18 RCMP officers (Mar 4, 2025 package presentation); RCMP invoice Oct-Dec 2024 $1,000,258 (Feb 4, 2025 package, accounts payable).
reasons: federal-sets-cost: city only chooses the number of officers; cost set by federal bargaining (Michael Zwaagstra); federal-sets-cost: the increase is the RCMP's own budget figure (Brian Hrehirchuk, Senior Manager, Finance)
vote: unanimous (B. Hiebert and Siemens excused Mar 4)
notes: Mar 4, 2025 public hearing on the financial plan; Siemens and B. Hiebert absent.

title: Second community safety officer in place
summary: In April 2025 council appointed one community safety officer as weed inspector; by March 2026 it appointed two, Grant Ryland and Kevin Williams, showing a second CSO had been added. In September 2026 the RCMP commander said CSOs helped with a Main Street traffic project and would likely enforce future e-bike rules.
status_detail: Weed-inspector appointments R25-076 (one CSO) and R25-052 [sic, March 3, 2026 minutes] (two CSOs), unanimous. The hiring decision itself isn't in the regular-meeting record (likely in the 2026 budget).
figures: 2025 budget presentation lists one 'Community Services Officer - City By-Laws' (Mar 4, 2025 package); two CSOs named Mar 3, 2026.
notes: The 2026 resolution number is printed 'R25-052' in the March 3, 2026 minutes, apparently a typo.

title: Bail reform: advocacy through the Cities Caucus and the regional committee
summary: Back from the AMM convention, the mayor said the Cities Caucus had made bail reform one of its five advocacy items and that a letter would go to the provincial justice minister about 'catch-and-release.' Councillor Jake Hiebert, a former RCMP officer, blamed ten years of 'catch and release' for making the public less safe. Councillor Siemens reported that the Eastman Regional Municipal Committee also writes letters supporting the major centres' push for bail reform.
status_detail: No council resolution or Steinbach letter on bail reform appears in the minutes; the advocacy ran through the Cities Caucus (AMM) and the ERMC (minutes Sep 16, 2025, item 21.3 lists bail reform among its issues).
figures: Province's 2% increase in policing funding to all municipalities (mayor, Apr 15, 2025 0:05:52).
reasons: root-causes-elsewhere: offenders are released the next day; bail is a provincial/federal matter (Mayor Earl Funk); root-causes-elsewhere: federal 'catch and release' made policing harder (Jake Hiebert)
notes: Justice Minister's name is mis-transcribed ('Wee'); not quoted.

title: Ste. Anne Police allowed to do MPI-funded traffic enforcement in Steinbach
summary: Councillor Zwaagstra reported more complaints about racing on Main Street and said the detachment was often two to four officers short. The acting detachment commander proposed joint enforcement with the Town of Ste. Anne's police, plus extra Ste. Anne patrols paid by Manitoba Public Insurance. Council agreed by consensus.
status_detail: Consensus of council (minutes item 29). Zwaagstra later cited the arrangement as 'not costing city taxpayers any money' (Jun 17, 2025). No results were reported to council.
figures: RCMP short 2-4 officers (Zwaagstra, 1:13:46; minutes item 28).
reasons: rcmp-cant-fill-positions: RCMP short 2-4 officers so other forces help (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Residents' reports of street racing on Main Street (as relayed by Zwaagstra).
notes: Details also in the traffic report.

title: 2025-26 RCMP priorities adopted unchanged
summary: Council adopted the detachment's 2025-26 community priorities: crime prevention (drugs), property crime, traffic, and communication/visibility of police. The mayor said they had barely changed in recent years and were worked out at the RCMP Advisory Committee.
status_detail: R25-108 carried unanimously. No numeric targets attached.
figures: Four priorities on the RCMP priorities form signed by the acting detachment commander (May 20, 2025 package).
reasons: already-doing-enough: priorities stay the same because they remain important (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Private overnight security hired with unspent RCMP money
summary: With the detachment running at about 14 to 15 of its 18 positions since 2022, council unanimously authorized administration to hire a private security firm, paid from the policing surplus. Councillors cited shortages across Canada, success with park patrols and private patrols hired by developers, and mostly 'small-scale and petty' crime.
status_detail: Steinbach Security Services started July 2, 2025: nightly 10 p.m.-6 a.m. patrols of construction sites and residential areas, month to month to Nov 30, 2025, paid from the unspent policing budget. Administration promised a fall report with RCMP statistics on petty theft and vandalism (minutes Jul 15, 2025, item 15).
figures: 18 authorized; about 15, just under 14, then 14.5 actual over three years, 15-25% short (Zwaagstra, 0:07:37).
reasons: rcmp-cant-fill-positions: adding a 19th position would not help because the RCMP can't fill 18 (Michael Zwaagstra); rcmp-cant-fill-positions: Manitoba Justice says shortages are national (Damian Penner); low-crime: most crime is small-scale and petty (Damian Penner)
public: Developers and business owners had met council about break-ins and theft at construction sites (mentioned by Siemens and the mayor).
notes: Jul 15, 2025 update (Thiessen) is from the minutes only; no transcript of that meeting.

title: Manitoba Crime Stoppers 2026 fundraising request received as information
summary: Manitoba Crime Stoppers' 2026 fundraising appeal came to council as correspondence and was received as information without discussion.
status_detail: Received as information (minutes item 19); no funding motion followed in the record through Oct 2026. Earlier Crime Stoppers requests (2023, 2025) were handled the same way.
public: Manitoba Crime Stoppers (organization).
notes: Amount requested not checked (package for Nov 4, 2025 not downloaded).

title: Overnight security patrol extended; $145,000 proposed for 2026
summary: Administration reported positive feedback from the RCMP and developers (less theft and vandalism; RCMP freed for higher-priority work) and recommended continuing the patrol until RCMP staffing can cover overnight property crime. Council extended it to the end of 2025 and put $145,000 forward for the 2026 budget.
status_detail: R25-209 unanimous. The evaluation was anecdotal: the July promise of a report with RCMP statistics on petty theft and vandalism was met with qualitative feedback only. The patrol continued through October 2026.
figures: $145,000 to continue in 2026 (Thiessen 0:04:32; minutes); 7 nights a week, 10 p.m.-6 a.m. (Thiessen 0:07:27).
reasons: cost: costs less than one RCMP officer (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: no extra money; reallocates the RCMP budget (Susan Penner)
public: Developers and business people had reported repeated break-ins and theft (as recounted by the mayor).
notes: Speaker C (patrol-hours question) is a merged Bill/Jake Hiebert label; not attributed.

title: Provincial Urban Policing Grant: $2.61 million (2025-26) and $2.67 million (2026-27)
summary: Manitoba Justice confirmed Urban Policing Grants that cover a large share of the RCMP bill. Council received both letters as information without discussion beyond the mayor noting the 2% increase.
status_detail: Received as information Dec 2, 2025 (minutes item 16) and Oct 20, 2026 (agenda 11C).
figures: $2,613,685 for 2025-26 (Dec 2, 2025 minutes); $2,665,959 for 2026-27, a 2% increase (Manitoba Justice letter Sept 15, 2026, Oct 20, 2026 package p. 96). RCMP quarterly invoice $1,000,258 (Feb 4, 2025 package).
notes: Oct 20, 2026 minutes not yet available; grant amount from the package letter.

title: First Street speeding letter sent to the RCMP Advisory Committee
summary: A resident (C.S.) asked for signage on First Street because of speeds and pedestrian traffic. The mayor asked Councillor Zwaagstra to raise patrolling there at the next day's RCMP Advisory Committee meeting.
status_detail: Consensus for Zwaagstra and the mayor to raise it at the RCMP advisory meeting (minutes item 23); no report back in the public record.
reasons: rcmp-job: speeding calls for policing rather than signs (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: C.S. letter requesting signage along First Street.
notes: The RCMP Advisory Committee's meetings are not public, so the outcome can't be checked.

title: Community Safety and Well-Being Plan published
summary: The city's Community Safety and Well-Being Plan, prepared by the Canadian Centre for Safer Communities from a resident survey, was added to the agenda and received as information. The mayor said Steinbach was the first of 11 funded Manitoba communities to finish its plan and that it mostly summarizes work local organizations already do.
status_detail: Received as information (minutes item 13), no adoption vote or implementation motion. In July 2026 staff said the province is funding plan initiatives with $60,000 directed by the plan's steering committee. The plan's actions (e.g. advocating for more RCMP and community safety officers) have timelines 'to be determined' (published plan).
figures: Survey of about 872 residents (mayor, 0:20:43; the published plan says 827); $60,000 provincial grant for plan initiatives (Thiessen, Jul 21, 2026 1:22:18).
reasons: already-doing-enough: the plan mostly summarizes what organizations already do (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: Survey participants reported a perceived lack of RCMP presence and unanswered 911 calls (published plan; residents' reports, unverified).
notes: Council joined the provincial CSWB planning process in 2024 (R24-025, outside this period).

title: 2026 budget keeps policing 'as usual' with no tax increase
summary: Council adopted the 2026 financial plan with the mill rate unchanged at 14.4. Councillor Zwaagstra said policing and fire services continue as usual. The transcript doesn't say whether the $145,000 security patrol was in the final budget; it ran all year.
status_detail: R26-058 unanimous. Complement stayed at 18.
figures: Mill rate 14.4 unchanged; capital $35.8 million (Hrehirchuk 0:08:40).

title: Resident links trespass and policing to a 48-unit rezoning
summary: At the hearing on a 48-unit building on McKenzie Avenue, H.K. described strangers walking through yards at night and said police had dismissed his call. No council member responded to the policing remarks.
status_detail: No council response on policing; the rezoning got second reading (see housing report).
public: H.K. (McKenzie Avenue): trespass at night, a dismissive police response; his account, unverified.
notes: Resident quote; not for public pages except by initials and in context.

title: $200,000 provincial public safety grant: truck and cameras proposed, decision deferred
summary: An unexpected $200,000 provincial grant arrived in April 2026.
